content: Providencia is a Gram-negative, motile bacterium belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae. Certain strains, such as Providencia stuartii, are opportunistic pathogens in humans and are known to cause urinary tract infections, particularly in patients with long-term indwelling urinary catheters or those with extensive severe burns. Other strains, such as Providencia burhodogranariea and Providencia sneebia, have been identified in the hemolymph of Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies. Some strains of Providencia are sensitive to ampicillin. Providencia stuartii is the most common species of Providencia capable of causing infections in humans. It is an opportunistic pathogen frequently observed in patients with severe burns or long-term indwelling urinary catheters, placing elderly individuals at a higher risk of infection. In animals, P. stuartii infections can lead to neonatal diarrhea, particularly in dairy cows. In humans, P. stuartii can be isolated from urine (most commonly), stool, blood, sputum, skin, and wound cultures. Bloodstream infections caused by P. stuartii are often of urinary origin. It is also the most common causative agent of purple urine bag syndrome. Clinical manifestations of P. stuartii bloodstream infections include fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. Providencia rettgeri is another Gram-negative bacterium commonly found in water and terrestrial environments. It can be cultured at 37°C using nutrient agar or nutrient broth. Strains of P. rettgeri have also been isolated from nematodes. This bacterium is capable of causing various opportunistic infections in humans and is a significant cause of traveler’s diarrhea. Additionally, P. rettgeri has been implicated in urinary tract infections and eye infections. P. rettgeri can be identified through its motility and its ability to produce acid from mannitol. It does not produce gas from glucose, does not ferment lactose, and does not produce hydrogen sulfide or acid from xylose. Treatment of Providencia infections often involves the removal of foreign materials, such as catheters, when applicable. For bacteremia, the recommended duration of treatment is 10–14 days or 3–5 days after defervescence and resolution of complicating factors. For acute prostatitis, the treatment duration is typically 2 weeks, whereas chronic prostatitis requires a longer course of 4–6 weeks.
